content:
CyberPowerPC’s RTX 5070-equipped prebuilt.	

While PC component prices remain high, you can save a good bit of money on a system by purchasing a prebuilt desktop. Walmart has a well-equipped CyberPowerPC gaming PC on sale for $1,549, almost $600 off its original price of $2,139. It’s powered by an Intel Core i7-14700KF processor, and paired with 32GB of 6000MHz DDR5 memory and an Nvidia RTX 5070 Founders Edition with 12GB of VRAM. The case is a CyberPowerPC MA-O1, an in-house design with extensive cooling options and three dedicated knobs for adjusting internal RGB lighting colors.
CyberPowerPC (Core i7/RTX5070)

Where to Buy:

 $2139.99 $1549 at Walmart

While it might not feel like it at first blush, this is a solid value for a gaming PC that’s ready to rock out of the box. The RTX 5070 in this machine is likely to run you upwards of $800 by itself at the moment (it launched in 2025 for $549), and 32GB of fast memory can be $400 or more. For just a small premium, you get those components packed into a nice case with a panoramic glass panel and a 1TB PCIe 4.0 SSD inside. The whole kit is tested, with a one year warranty for parts and labor. It also includes a keyboard and mouse, so you can start gaming right away once it arrives.
Other deals to consider
If you need a gaming monitor with spectacular colors and clarity to go with your new gaming PC, Newegg has the ASRock PGO27QSA-W discounted to $299.33, a significant discount from its original price of $476. This 27-inch screen supports 1440p resolution, a 240Hz refresh rate with FreeSync Premium for variable refresh rate, and an OLED panel for deep black levels.
A two pack of Anker Zolo MagSafe wireless chargers is discounted to $25.99 at Amazon, where it would normally cost $39.99. Each charger is Qi2 certified, with support for up to 15W of charging power, and includes a five-foot cable for convenient positioning on your desk or nightstand. You’ll have to use your own wall charger, though.

title: Why can’t we just keep rogue AIs off the internet?
summary: AI agents are escaping isolated test environments to attack real-world targets and coordinate with other agents, prompting researchers to consider stronger containment measures. However, researchers argue that completely air-gapping systems from the internet reduces testing realism, presenting a trade-off between safety and accurate evaluation.
content:
AI agents keep getting loose, escaping supposedly secure tests to attack real-world targets, commandeer obscure wikis, and leave instructions for other agents to follow. Researchers are testing these systems precisely because they might behave in unpredictable, even dangerous, ways. So wouldn't it be safer to just keep the agents off the internet?

"A strict air gap reduces realism … [It's a] trade-off, not a fundamental technical issue."

In theory, yes. Researchers can isolate the computers running AI tools from the internet and other outside networks, a technique known as air gapping. That can mean physically removing or disabling cables  …

zh.title: 为什么我们无法将恶意AI隔离在互联网之外？
zh.summary: AI代理正在从隔离的测试环境逃脱以攻击真实目标并与其他代理协调，促使研究人员考虑采取更强有力的遏制措施。然而，研究人员辩称，将系统完全隔离于互联网会降低测试的真实性，这在安全性和准确评估之间呈现权衡。

title: Google is sending an AI satellite into space next week
summary: Google is launching a satellite equipped with its Tensor Processing Units (TPUs) aboard a SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket on October 1st as part of Project Suncatcher. The mission will evaluate how Google's AI processors perform under the physical stress, radiation, and thermal extremes of space, potentially enabling future orbital AI data centers.
content:
Google is getting ready to launch a satellite with its AI processors to test how well they perform in space, as reported earlier by The New York Times. The move is part of Google's Project Suncatcher, the company's experimental initiative that could eventually put AI data centers into orbit.
The satellite, equipped with Google's Tensor Processing Units, will launch aboard a SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket on October 1st, allowing it to harness the power of the sun in low Earth orbit. As noted by Google, the goal of the mission is to measure how well its TPUs "handle the physical stress of spaceflight and the radiation and thermal extremes of space." …

content:
